What percentage of the individuals in the dataset are children?

Plot the relationship between donuts and weight

plot(donutd$donuts, donutd$weight) #scatterplot (X then Y)
abline(lm(donutd$weight~donutd$donuts)) #add trend line (Y then X)

Make plot look a bit more respectable

plot(donutd$donuts, donutd$weight, main="Relationship between Donut Consumption and Weight", xlab="Donuts", ylab="Weight")
abline(lm(donutd$weight~donutd$donuts)) #and boom, you've already ran your 2nd regression
text(donutd$donuts, donutd$weight-12, donutd$name)#add labels(the -12 is to offset the label)

Does there appear to be a relationship in the sample?

What about with just males? There are multiple ways to do this:

First, off we don’t think we’ll reuse the dataset we can pull out what we need in the code

plot(donutd$donuts[donutd$male==0], donutd$weight[donutd$male==0], main="Relationship between Donut Consumption and Weight(Males Only)", xlab="Donuts", ylab="Weight") #The [donutd$male==1] is telling R to only include dots where male=1, ie only males.
abline(lm(donutd$weight[donutd$male==0]~donutd$donuts[donutd$male==0])) #

Or we can create a new dataset(I usually choose this option)

males <- donutd[which(donutd$male==0),]

plot(males$donuts, males$weight, main="Relationship between Donut Consumption and Weight", xlab="Donuts", ylab="Weight")
abline(lm(males$weight~males$donuts)) #and boom, you've already ran your 2nd regression
text(males$donuts, males$weight-12, males$name)

Heads Up: We will practice this a third way using the dplyr package in the coming weeks

Other ways to subset:

Exclude kids

adults <- donutd[which(donutd$child!=-1),] # the != does not equal

Exclude overweight

normweight <- donutd[which(donutd$weight< 250),] # the

Try creating a scatterplot with just the 1) females 2) characters who at least eat donuts.

donuteaters <- donutd[which(donutd$donuts> 0),]

plot(donuteaters$donuts, donuteaters$weight, main="Relationship between Donut Consumption and Weight", sub="Donut Eaters", xlab="Donuts", ylab="Weight")
abline(lm(donuteaters$weight~donuteaters$donuts)) #and boom, you've already ran your 2nd regression
text(donuteaters$donuts, donuteaters$weight-12, donuteaters$name)

#Looking at a different dataset: Time to look at something a bit more fun. World cup players. The data are from this article: https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/world-cup-comparisons/landon-donovan-2010/

We want to load a csv file into R. Here’s how you do it. Make that sure when you do this, your data is in the same working directory that you set your assignment in(This allows us to avoid typing out the whole file path). It is easy to save excel files as csv

wc <- read.csv("wc.csv", header=T)

Different file formats have different load commands. If your data is already saved as an .RData file (hint hint, check the problem set data), then run this code:load(“name_of_data_set.RData”) We’re not going to run it here, because we only have a CSV dataset.

R can load excel, spss, stata, text, etc. if you use the right command.

Remember all these indicators are z-standardized.

#creating new variables

What if we wanted to an aggregrate indicator for how aggressive each player is on offense.

R understands standard addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, etc.

wc$off <- wc$progpasses_z + wc$progruns_z
mean(wc$off) #doesn't mean much because z-scored
## [1] -1.017122e-05
min(wc$off)
## [1] -2.39
max(wc$ofF)
## Warning in max(wc$ofF): no non-missing arguments to max; returning -Inf
## [1] -Inf
#lets add crosses and take ons and then average the z-score. Notice R is following the order of operations
wc$offplus <- (wc$off + wc$crosses_z + wc$takeons_z)/4
summary(wc$offplus)
##      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
## -1.005000 -0.537500 -0.187500 -0.000097  0.345000  5.050000
hist(wc$offplus)

Let’s make a simple scatterplot with expected goals in the horizontal axis, and goals on the vertical axis, with labels. Let’s type out a regression (Looking at the relationship between variables), and then let’s add a regression line linear regression model, and you’re looking at the effect of the IV on the DV

plot(wc$xg_z, wc$goals_z, ylab = "Goals", xlab = "Expected Goals", main = "Goals Based on Expected Gobals")
abline(lm(wc$goals_z ~ wc$xg_z), col="red") # What type of relationship is this?
abline(v=mean(wc$xg_z), col="blue")

That is a bit overwhelming lets just look at the most recent world cup

france18 <- wc[which(wc$season==2018),]
plot(france18$xg_z, france18$goals_z, ylab = "Goals", xlab = "Expected Goals", main = "Goals Based on Expected Gobals")
abline(lm(france18$goals_z ~ france18$xg_z), col="red")


france18$stars <- ifelse(france18$player=="Lionel Messi"|france18$player=="Cristiano Ronaldo", france18$player, "")
text(france18$xg_z, france18$goals_z-.2, france18$stars, cex=.4)

plot(france18$xg_z, france18$goals_z, ylab = "Goals", xlab = "Expected Goals", main = "Goals Based on Expected Gobals", col=as.factor(france18$team), pch=10)
abline(lm(france18$goals_z ~ france18$xg_z), col="red")

france18$stars2 <- ifelse(france18$player=="Lionel Messi"|france18$player=="Cristiano Ronaldo"|france18$player=="Mohamed Salah"|france18$player=="Luka Modric"|france18$player=="Paul Pogba", france18$player, "")
text(france18$xg_z, france18$goals_z-.35, france18$stars2, cex=.8) #cex is text size

I’ve clearly had too much fun. Your turn to make something cool

Since we’ve created some new variables we may want to save our data:

write.csv(wc, "wcv2.csv") #writes a csv to your working directory
save(wc, file="wcv2.RData") #saves Rdata format to your working directory

Note: you can open this new file in excel

Challenge: Create a plot for a single team(country+year) and create an interesting plot with player names
